{"needs":[{"challengeId":"C004-CH1","triage":"research","triageReason":"The company faces an open technical problem in spatial interpolation and sensor fusion: how to combine multiple weather data sources (ground stations 30 km apart, private networks, satellite soil moisture indices) into a single spatially accurate rainfall estimate per plot that improves on current station-based thresholds.","restatement":{"text":"OsiguroMi's parametric crop insurance pays claims when the nearest official weather station records rainfall below a contractual threshold, but stations are sometimes 30 km from the plot, missing local rainfall variation caused by terrain (mountains, valleys, urban zones) (C004-CH1). The company receives feedback that payouts occur when fields remain dry and are withheld when crops are lost. The company has access to RHMZS data and three private agrometeorological networks totalling around 140 measurement points in the region, and has considered satellite soil-moisture indices, but is uncertain how to reliably combine these sources into a single trigger (C004-CH1). The goal is to correct payouts by the next season using spatially more accurate rainfall estimates per plot without fully replacing the contracted threshold (C004-CH1).","sourceIds":["C004-CH1"]},"searchTerms":["spatial interpolation","kriging","rain gauge networks","satellite soil moisture","sensor fusion","weather data assimilation","precipitation downscaling","microclimate estimation","multi-source data integration","agricultural drought index"],"assets":[{"text":"RHMZS data and data from three private agrometeorological networks totalling around 140 measurement points in the region (C004-CH1).","sourceIds":["C004-CH1"]},{"text":"Satellite soil-moisture indices that the company has considered (C004-CH1).","sourceIds":["C004-CH1"]},{"text":"One internal researcher for data modelling and two senior engineers who can allocate a portion of their capacity to joint projects, on the condition that results are applicable within six to nine months (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]},{"text":"Access to feedback from partners in Vojvodina and Bačka about crop losses and payout accuracy (C004-CH1).","sourceIds":["C004-CH1"]},{"text":"PostgreSQL databases with time series for historical losses (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]}],"constraints":[{"text":"The goal is to correct payouts by the next season, without completely replacing the contracted threshold (C004-CH1).","sourceIds":["C004-CH1"]},{"text":"Results must be applicable within six to nine months (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]},{"text":"The company plans to expand the agro line to Bulgaria and Romania through partnerships with regional cooperatives by the end of 2025 (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]}]},{"challengeId":"C004-CH2","triage":"research","triageReason":"The company has a data quality problem in real-time streams: 3.1% of automated flight-delay payouts are triggered by API errors (duplicate entries, timestamp errors, status misclassifications) rather than genuine delays. The company has a log of all previous API calls and payouts totalling around 340,000 entries (C004-CH2). The company attempted simple anomaly-detection rules but false alarms block legitimate payouts (C004-CH2). A method is needed that can assess credibility of incoming data before the trigger activates payout in real time (under 60 seconds), working within existing infrastructure without building a new system from scratch (C004-CH2).","sourceIds":["C004-CH2"]},"searchTerms":["anomaly detection","data quality","real-time validation","API data credibility","outlier detection","consistency checking","time-series anomalies","rule-based filtering","event stream validation","false positive reduction"],"assets":[{"text":"A log of all previous API calls and payouts, totalling around 340,000 entries (C004-CH2).","sourceIds":["C004-CH2"]},{"text":"Integration with an external flight-status API (FlightBridge Data Services) (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]},{"text":"Automated rules-based claims processing (rules engine) currently in place (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]},{"text":"One internal researcher for data modelling and two senior engineers who can allocate a portion of their capacity to joint projects, on the condition that results are applicable within six to nine months (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]},{"text":"PostgreSQL databases with time series for historical losses (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]}],"constraints":[{"text":"The budget for this is not unlimited; the company is looking for a solution that can operate within existing infrastructure, not a new system built from scratch (C004-CH2).","sourceIds":["C004-CH2"]},{"text":"The decision must be made in under 60 seconds from the moment the flight status API reports a change, because the whole point of the product is that the user receives a notification before leaving the airport (C004-CH2).","sourceIds":["C004-CH2"]},{"text":"Results must be applicable within six to nine months (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]},{"text":"Kubernetes orchestration for scaling during peak booking traffic is in place (C004).","sourceIds":["C004"]}]},{"challengeId":"C004-CH3","triage":"research","triageReason":"The company faces a small-sample statistical problem in actuarial science: with fewer than 200 historical festival events in the database, standard actuarial methods produce unstable loss curves. The research question is how to build stable pricing models using extreme-value statistics, broader meteorological data, and bottom-up reconstruction to yield reasonable confidence intervals despite the limited event history.","restatement":{"text":"OsiguroMi is developing parametric insurance for open-air festival organisers, where the policy is triggered if precipitation forecast exceeds a threshold on event days or authorities prohibit the event due to weather (C004-CH3). To set prices, the company needs stable loss curves, but its database contains just under 200 historical festival events in the region with accompanying weather data—too few for classical actuarial methods, and loss curves are unstable (C004-CH3). {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"OsiguroMi d.o.o. is an insurtech company from Novi Sad, founded in 2019 with one idea: that insurance should stop being paperwork and become a silent service embedded in the tools people already use. Instead of a user buying a policy on a separate website, our technology integrates directly into travel booking applications, agro-platforms and ticket-sales systems of festival organisers — and the policy is created at the moment of the transaction. We work with B2B partners across Serbia and the EU: travel platforms, cooperatives, organisers of open-air events. Our team of 58 employees comes from insurance, software engineering and data analysis. Founders Milena Čabarkapa and Dragan Horvat previously worked in reinsurance and the fintech sector, which shaped our approach: model first, then product. What sets us apart is not marketing — what sets us apart is an API that can be switched on in less than one working day and parametric triggers that do not require a claim request from the user. A payout happens automatically or it does not, based on measurable data: flight delay, rainfall amount, event cancellation. No forms, no waiting. Our partners' clients rarely notice it until they need it, and then they notice it immediately."},{"line":2,"english":"Products: Parametric crop insurance based on weather triggers; Automatic flight-delay insurance embedded in booking platforms; Festival and open-air event cancellation insurance; White-label API for embedding micro-insurance in third-party applications; B2B partner dashboard with real-time payout analytics."},{"line":3,"english":"Tech: REST API with OAuth 2.0 authentication for partner integrations; Automated rules-based claims processing (rules engine); Integration with an external flight-status API (FlightBridge Data Services); Network of weather stations and RHMZS data for agro-products; PostgreSQL databases with time series for historical losses; Python environment for actuarial modelling and trigger calibration; Kubernetes orchestration for scaling during peak booking traffic."},{"line":4,"english":"Plans: By the end of 2025 we plan to expand the agro line to Bulgaria and Romania through partnerships with regional cooperatives, and to introduce a new trigger for frost insurance. We are also considering the possibility of our own licensed distribution in one additional EU jurisdiction in order to reduce dependence on external intermediaries."},{"line":5,"english":"R&D capacity: We have one internal researcher for data modelling and two senior engineers who can allocate a portion of their capacity to joint projects, on the condition that results are applicable within six to nine months."},{"line":6,"english":"Past collaborations: In 2022 we collaborated with a local software firm, Logosfera d.o.o., on the development of a prototype partner dashboard, but formal research collaboration with academic institutions has not been established to date."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Our agro-product pays out a benefit when the official meteorological station records a rainfall amount below the contracted threshold in a given period. The problem is that the nearest station is sometimes 30 kilometres from the plot — and across those 30 km there can be a mountain range, a river valley or an urban zone, all of which drastically alter local rainfall. We are receiving feedback from partners in Vojvodina and Bačka that payouts reached them when the field had not even dried out, or that there were none when they had lost their crop. We tried to correct the threshold on the basis of historical differences between stations and terrain, but that is a rough approximation. We have access to RHMZS data and data from three private agrometeorological networks, totalling around 140 measurement points in the region. We have been considering satellite soil-moisture indices, but we are not certain how to reliably combine those sources into a single trigger. The aim is to correct payouts by the next season on the basis of spatially more accurate rainfall estimates per plot, without completely replacing the contracted threshold."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"We process around 9,000 flight-delay compensation claims per month, fully automatically, without human review. The internal audit for Q3 2023 showed that 3.1% of payouts were triggered by data errors from the flight-status data provider — incorrect timestamps, duplicate entries, flights that were technically cancelled but displayed as delayed. That is not a negligible percentage when we are talking about payouts in euros. We currently work with a single external flight-status API. We attempted to introduce simple anomaly-detection rules, but false alarms block legitimate payouts. We need a method that can assess the credibility of incoming data before the trigger activates a payout — preferably in real time, because the whole point of the product is that the user receives a notification before leaving the airport. We have a log of all previous API calls and payouts, which amounts to around 340,000 entries in total. The budget for this is not unlimited — we are looking for a solution that can operate within our existing infrastructure, not a new system built from scratch."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"We are developing parametric insurance for open-air festival organisers: the policy is triggered if the precipitation forecast exceeds a threshold on event days, or if the authorities prohibit the event from taking place due to weather conditions. To set the price, we need stable loss curves. Our database contains just under 200 historical festival events in the region with accompanying weather data — that is too few for classical actuarial methods, the curves are unstable and the margins we need to charge become uncompetitive. We tried to supplement the database with data from open sources and news archives, but the quality and consistency are uneven. We are considering making broader use of meteorological data — for example, extreme-value statistics for each region and season — and building the model from the bottom up rather than purely from event history. We do not have the capacity to carry this through to completion on our own, as our actuarial team numbers two people. Concrete goal: a pricing methodology that yields reasonable confidence intervals even with a small set of historical events, applicable to different locations in the region."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"We signed a distribution agreement with the Vienna-based travel booking platform ViennaJourney GmbH and were supposed to start selling in the first quarter of 2024. However, the process of obtaining a licence from the Austrian regulator FMA has been stalled for seven months. Our legal representative who was handling the case submitted their resignation last summer and the documentation was left incomplete. We found a new adviser, but the procedure is starting practically from scratch because FMA requires certain documents certified by the person who originally submitted the application. This is a regulatory, not a technical, problem — but it has a direct impact on revenue because ViennaJourney GmbH has included our product in its plan for the summer season. We are not looking for shortcuts; we are looking for someone who knows the FMA procedure from the inside and who can help us put the documentation together in a way that will not be sent back for a third time. Time pressure exists: if we do not obtain the licence by May 2024, the partner will push the integration back by an entire season."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"OsiguroMi d.o.o. and the farm management platform Polje.rs have signed a partnership agreement by which parametric crop insurance is integrated directly into the Polje.rs mobile application. Under the terms of the cooperation, users of the Polje.rs platform can activate a weather policy for their plot with two clicks in the application — without visiting an agent, without paperwork. The policy is linked to the user's cadastral parcel and tracks precipitation based on available meteorological data for the corresponding microzone. In the first phase, which began on 1 November 2023, coverage is available for farms in Vojvodina and Mačva. Expansion to the rest of Serbia is planned for the second half of 2024. The director of the Polje.rs platform, Aleksandar Mišković, stated: 'Our users have been asking for years for a solution that works without bureaucracy. This is concrete and measurable.' According to internal data from the OsiguroMi team, approximately 1,200 policies were activated in the first 30 days since launch. The trigger season for winter wheat begins in April 2024. This integration is the first in the agro-sector for OsiguroMi and marks the company's entry into a market it has not previously covered. The next step is calibration of the model based on feedback arriving from farms during the pilot period."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"OsiguroMi is an API-first platform for embedding parametric micro-insurance. Our partners are platforms, applications and B2B services that want to offer insurance as part of their product — without needing to become an insurer themselves. How it works: a partner integrates our API into their checkout or booking page. When a user completes a reservation, our system automatically generates a policy based on the transaction parameters — destination, date, value, plot location and similar. The policy is sent to the user within a few seconds. If a trigger occurs — a flight is delayed beyond a defined threshold, rainfall falls below the contracted limit, an event is cancelled — payment is initiated without any claim on the part of the user. Our B2B partners today include the travel agency MontFlite from Belgrade, the agro-platform Polje.rs and the festival organiser SoundRavine Events. Through their channels, our policies are active with more than 40,000 end users. Technical characteristics of our integration:"},{"line":2,"english":"— Sandbox environment for testing without real data"},{"line":3,"english":"— Webhooks for real-time notifications"},{"line":4,"english":"— SLA of 99.7% availability We support integrations within one business day for standard use cases. For non-standard triggers or new market segments, we work through a pilot programme lasting four to six weeks. We are not a broker or intermediary in the classical sense — we are the technological and actuarial layer that sits between the reinsurer and digital distribution channels. Each of our products is covered by a contract with a reinsurer before it goes to market."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"When we completed the internal payout audit for the third quarter in October 2023, the number that stood out was 3.1%. That is how many of our automatic flight delay payouts should not have been triggered — not due to a policy error, not due to customer fraud, but due to bad data that entered the system before the trigger had even checked anything. Our claims processing mechanism works fast because it has to. A customer delayed on a flight needs a notification while they are still at the airport. That means the system makes a decision in under 60 seconds from the moment the flight status API reports a change. The problem is that this API sometimes reports changes that are artefacts of the system, not reality — duplicate entries, a flight reclassified from 'cancelled' to 'delayed' for operator technical reasons, timestamps that do not correspond to the actual gate status. In absolute numbers, 3.1% of 9,000 monthly claims means approximately 279 incorrect payouts per month. Each payout in this category amounts to between 15 and 60 EUR. It is not a disaster, but it is a systematic drain that accumulates. What we did not have is a filter that would check the consistency of incoming data before the trigger. We are now looking for exactly that: not a system that slows down processing, but a validation layer that can identify implausible combinations of data and either send them for a short manual review or hold them for 90 seconds until confirmation arrives from an alternative source. If you work on problems like these or have experience with anomaly detection in real-time API streams, we are open to a conversation."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Evaluation of Large Language Models on Legal Reasoning Tasks in the Serbian Language (2025, conference, Language, Technology and Law – Proceedings of the Second Conference on Computational Linguistics for the Serbian Language)."},{"line":2,"english":"The paper systematically evaluates the capability of four large language models (LLMs) – GPT-4o, Llama 3 70B, Mistral Large, and the Serbian-adapted model SrbGPT-7B – on a set of legal reasoning tasks in the Serbian language. Five tasks were defined: identification of the relevant legal basis, detection of violations of procedural norms, extraction of parties to a dispute, summarisation of a judgment in a prescribed format, and classification into a legal domain. Each task covers 200 examples, manually verified by legal experts. GPT-4o achieves the highest accuracy on four out of five tasks (73–89%), while SrbGPT-7B, despite having far fewer parameters, achieves competitive results on the morphologically more demanding extraction tasks. The paper identifies systematic errors in the understanding of negation and reference to previous statements (anaphora resolution) as a common problem across all models. The conclusions are relevant for assessing the practical applicability of LLMs in a judicial context."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Measuring Semantic Similarity between Serbian Legal Norms and Corporate Policies: A Contrastive Learning Approach (2023, conference, Proceedings of the 9th Central European Conference on Information and Intelligent Systems (CECIIS))."},{"line":2,"english":"This paper addresses the problem of automatically matching legal norms from domestic legislation with internal corporate policies for the purpose of compliance verification. A contrastive learning approach is proposed in which positive pairs were manually defined by compliance consultants, and negative pairs were sampled from different legal domains. The model uses a dual-encoder with Serbian RoBERTa initialization, fine-tuned on 3,200 annotated pairs. The evaluation covers both the standard precision on the test set (mAP = 0.79) and a practical metric defended before business users: the proportion of cases in which the correct law was ranked within the top three results (Recall@3 = 0.88). Comparison with BM25 and standard cosine similarity on SBERT vectors indicates an improvement of 9 and 5 percentage points, respectively, for Recall@3. The model was integrated into a prototype compliance tool that was tested in two companies from the financial sector."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Anomaly Detection in Public Procurement Using Text Processing and Statistical Modelling Methods (2017, journal, Proceedings of FTN – Electrical Engineering and Computer Science)."},{"line":2,"english":"The paper describes a system for the automatic detection of potentially irregular tender documents in the public procurement database of the Republic of Serbia. A set of 23,400 tender specifications published between 2013 and 2016 was used. Anomalies are defined in three categories: unusual technical conditions that restrict competition, inconsistent use of units of measurement and values, and copying of text between apparently unrelated bids. For the detection of the first category, a one-class SVM was applied to TF-IDF vectors; for the second, a statistical control chart based on the z-score of numerically extracted values was used; for the third, fuzzy hashing (MinHash LSH). The system was validated on 200 manually reviewed examples by auditors of the State Audit Institution, achieving a recall of 0.83 and a precision of 0.61. The paper discusses limitations caused by the quality of the original OCR documents."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Named Entity Recognition in Serbian Court Decisions: Comparison of Conditional Random Fields and Transformer Models (2021, conference, Proceedings of the International Conference INFOTEH-Jahorina)."},{"line":2,"english":"The paper compares conditional random fields (CRF) and two transformer models (multilingual BERT and Serbian RoBERTa) on the task of named entity recognition in a corpus of 2,100 anonymised first-instance judgements from the field of criminal law. Eight entity types were defined: person, organisation, location, date, court reference, legal provision, monetary amount, and penal measure. The CRF model achieves an F1 of 0.78, multilingual BERT 0.84, and Serbian RoBERTa 0.87, measured as the micro-average across all types. The greatest relative improvement of the transformer models is recorded for the type 'legal provision' (F1 rises from 0.61 to 0.83). The paper describes particular challenges in anonymised texts where personal names have been replaced with labels, which makes coreference resolution more difficult. A detailed error analysis by entity type is provided."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Semi-supervised learning for the categorisation of legislative amendments in the Serbian legal system (2014, journal, Računarstvo i informatika – časopis za teoriju i primenu računarskih nauka)."},{"line":2,"english":"This paper investigates the application of semi-supervised classification methods to the problem of automatically recognising types of amendments in legislative texts (additions, deletions, substitutions and terminological changes). The initial set of labelled examples comprises 620 manually annotated paragraphs from the Official Gazette of the RS for the period 2008–2012, while the semi-supervised component relies on 14,000 unlabelled paragraphs. Three approaches were tested: self-training, co-training with two views (lexical and syntactic), and graph-based label propagation. Co-training achieves a macro F1 of 0.74 compared to 0.68 for the purely supervised model with the same amount of labelled data. The paper analyses the effect of the size of the initial labeled set (50, 200 and 620 examples) on the stability of the results and proposes a heuristic for selecting reliable self-labelled examples."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"The study analyses how different levels of disagreement between annotators affect the performance of classification models in the Serbian legal domain. The experiment uses three differently annotated versions of the same corpus of 3,600 documents: the first annotated by legal experts (high consistency, kappa = 0.82), the second by law students (medium consistency, kappa = 0.67), and the third by general users via a platform similar to the crowdsourcing model (low consistency, kappa = 0.54). Logistic regression, Random Forest, and a BERT-based model were trained on each version. The results show that the difference in the F1 measure between expert and crowdsourced annotation ranges between 3.1 and 7.8 percentage points, depending on the model and legal category. The BERT model demonstrates greater robustness to noisy labels than classical models. The implications for the practical organisation of annotation projects in the legal domain are discussed."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"The paper presents a system for the automatic classification of court decisions of the Supreme Court of Cassation of the Republic of Serbia into 12 legal areas. The corpus consists of 4,200 anonymised decisions collected between 2003 and 2008. An SVM classifier with a linear kernel was applied to TF-IDF vectorised texts, with experimentation involving different n-gram sizes (unigrams, bigrams and trigrams). Evaluation was carried out using fivefold cross-validation. The best result was achieved with a combination of unigrams and bigrams: the macro F1 score was 0.81. The error analysis shows that categories with a small number of examples and ambiguous terminology (e.g. labour law versus commercial law) are the most difficult to distinguish. The paper also describes the annotation procedure and the inter-annotator agreement metric (Cohen's kappa = 0.79)."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Partners: NTP Novi Sad – portfolio company RegTech Solutions d.o.o. (fictitious); Energodata Consulting d.o.o., Novi Sad (fictitious); Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad."},{"line":2,"english":"The project develops a prototype SaaS tool that enables small and medium-sized enterprises in the energy and financial sectors to automatically verify the compliance of internal documents with relevant legal regulations. The technical core consists of a semantic similarity model trained with contrastive learning, supplemented by a module for the detection of out-of-distribution documents. The system is integrated with the search of legal databases via API and presents results through a web interface with sentence-level explanations. Two business partners participate in the project, providing real test documents and taking part in the evaluation of the prototype under production conditions."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Bio: Ksenija Mitrović graduated from the Faculty of Technical Sciences of the University of Novi Sad in 2001, where she also defended her doctoral dissertation in 2009 in the field of natural language processing for the classification of legal documents. From 2011 she works as an assistant professor, and from 2018 as a full professor at the Department of Computing and Control Engineering. Her research group deals with supervised and semi-supervised learning for semantic similarity and anomaly detection in domain-specific textual corpora, primarily in the legal and regulatory domain. She teaches courses in machine learning and natural language processing at master's and doctoral studies. The laboratory uses a cluster with GPU nodes and tools such as spaCy, Hugging Face Transformers, and Elasticsearch."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Building an inverted index for Serbian texts with mixed script: core methodology (2010, conference, Proceedings of the Conference on the Application of Computers and the Internet in Serbia (PRIS 2010))."},{"line":2,"english":"The paper describes a methodology for building an inverted index that simultaneously processes Cyrillic and Latin occurrences of Serbian words without prior complete conversion into a single script. The proposed procedure includes a token normalisation step by which a canonical form based on phonemic representation is generated for each token, and the phonemic keys are then used as primary identifiers in the index. Experiments were conducted on a corpus of 120,000 newspaper articles collected from three Serbian daily newspapers in the period 2000–2008. Precision and recall measures were compared with two baseline systems that use exclusively a Cyrillic, and exclusively a Latin index, respectively. The proposed system achieves an F1 value of 0.81 on the ad-hoc retrieval task, which is an increase of 14 percentage points relative to the better of the two baseline systems. The paper also considers the question of the memory footprint of the hybrid index and proposes a vocabulary compression strategy."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Automatic Detection and Correction of Script Inconsistencies in Serbian Digital Archives (2015, conference, Proceedings of the 23rd Telecommunications Forum TELFOR)."},{"line":2,"english":"Digital archives of Serbian newspapers and institutional documents frequently contain inconsistencies where the same document is partly in Cyrillic and partly in Latin script, sometimes due to scanning errors or editorial interventions. This paper proposes a method for automatic detection of such inconsistencies at the sentence level, using a classifier that takes as features the distribution of script blocks, bigram frequencies, and morphosyntactic signals. The classifier was trained on 9,400 manually annotated sentences from the archive of a Novi Sad newspaper and tested on 2,100 sentences from the archive of a Belgrade newspaper. It achieves a precision of 0.91 and a recall of 0.88 on the class of inconsistent sentences. The correction step applies phonemic transliteration to the detected inconsistent tokens. A downstream experiment (document retrieval) shows that the corrected version of the archive yields higher accuracy than the uncorrected one by 7 percentage points in average precision."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Real-time search over a Serbian-language news stream with mixed script (2022, journal, Informatika i sistemi: Časopis za informacione tehnologije i računarstvo)."},{"line":2,"english":"Real-time search systems over news streams require incremental index updates with low latency. When a news stream comes from multiple sources that use different scripts, the incremental indexer must normalise the script of each incoming item before insertion. This paper describes the architecture of a system that processes up to 1,200 news articles per minute, with an average indexing latency of 340 ms on a single server node with 16 cores. Script normalisation and phonemic canonicalisation are implemented as a parallel pipeline that adds less than 15% time overhead compared to a system without normalisation. Search precision evaluation was conducted on a simulated stream of 2.1 million articles collected over 30 days. The system is scalable and can be horizontally scaled by adding normalisation nodes independently of indexing nodes."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Bio: Stefan Dragić graduated in mathematics from the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Novi Sad in 2001, and received his doctorate in 2008 from the same faculty, with a thesis on indexing multi-script text corpora. After a postdoctoral stay at the University of Vienna (2009–2010), he returned to the Department of Mathematics and Informatics, where in 2019 he was appointed to the rank of full professor. His research group works on information retrieval in documents containing mixed Cyrillic-Latin Serbian script, script normalization, transliteration as a preprocessing step, and the construction of inverted indexes robust to script variations. He teaches courses in database management and text mining. The laboratory uses its own corpora of legal and journalistic texts."},{"line":2,"english":"Industry experience: In the period 2022–2023, he collaborated with a Novi Sad-based legaltech startup on the adaptation of a search module for Serbian court decisions, within the framework of a contract research engagement lasting 18 months."},{"line":3,"english":"Notes: Dragić prefers collaboration with companies that have a clearly defined and sufficiently large text corpus in the Serbian language; he is not interested in general software development projects without a research component. He is currently engaged in two active projects, but has capacity for one smaller industrial contract or consulting engagement."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Script normalization in the context of internal document search engines for small and medium enterprises: experiences from practice (2024, conference, Proceedings of the SYmposium on Informatics and Applied Mathematics (SIAM-Serbia 2024))."},{"line":2,"english":"Small and medium enterprises in Serbia store internal documents — contracts, minutes, reports — in mixed script without a consistent policy. This paper describes experiences from three pilot implementations of internal search based on an open-source search framework supplemented with a script normalization module developed within our research group. The pilot companies had collections of between 8,000 and 45,000 documents. We measured search precision before and after the introduction of normalization, user response, and implementation costs. In all cases normalization improved precision by at least 11 percentage points. The administrative costs of implementation were low because the module was integrated as a plug-in without modifying the rest of the system. The paper also identifies limitations: the module needs to be updated when a company introduces new terminology in one script, because the initial synonym dictionary is not complete."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"The Impact of Morphological Reduction on the Precision of Retrieval of Serbian Multi-Script Documents (2013, journal, Infoteka: Journal of Informatics and Library Science)."},{"line":2,"english":"Keywords: morphological analysis; stemming; multi-script text; Serbian language; ranking."},{"line":3,"english":"The Serbian language is morphologically rich, meaning that the same lexeme can have several dozen inflectional forms. In this paper we examine how stemming and lemmatisation interact with the script normalisation procedure in the construction of a search index. We use three stemmers available for the Serbian language — two rule-based and one statistical — and combine them with a phonemic canonicalisation step described in previous papers. The evaluation was carried out on a subset of the CLEF 2012 collection containing documents in both scripts. The results show that the order of operations (stemming before or after script normalisation) affects recall, whereby stemming after normalisation consistently yields better results for all three combinations (an improvement of 4 to 9 percentage points in MAP). The paper also provides an error analysis for 50 manually reviewed queries."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Formal Verification of a Firmware Delivery Protocol by Model Checking (2013, conference, Proceedings of the Telecommunications Forum TELFOR)."},{"line":2,"english":"Keywords: formal verification; SPIN; Promelamodel checking; firmware protocol; LTL."},{"line":3,"english":"In this paper the model checking tool SPIN is applied to a protocol for authenticated firmware delivery in wireless telemetry networks. The protocol was modelled in the Promela language, and the verification covered 14 security and liveness properties formulated in linear temporal logic. Three conditions were found in which replay of an old message can lead to the installation of a previous firmware version if the monotonic sequence counter is reset after a device reset. An extension of the protocol with a persistent counter in a protected non-volatile memory area is proposed. The corrected protocol was verified without violation of the stated properties in a state space of up to 2.1 × 10⁸ states. The paper also discusses the limitations of abstracting cryptographic primitives in the SPIN model and proposes a methodology for separate modelling of protocol logic and cryptographic assumptions."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Fields: Telecommunications and wireless networks; Security of embedded systems; Industrial informatics and telemetry; Cryptographic protocols."},{"line":2,"english":"Bio: Ana Rajić is a full professor at the Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications of the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad. She graduated in 2001 and received her doctorate in 2009 at the same faculty, with a thesis on protocols for secure firmware distribution in industrial networks with limited bandwidth. Her research group works on firmware authentication and integrity in telemetry systems with intermittent wireless connectivity, including LPWAN technologies and industrial SCADA environments. She teaches courses in embedded systems security and wireless network protocols. The laboratory is equipped with degraded-channel emulation equipment, LoRaWAN and Zigbee development platforms, as well as tools for formal verification of cryptographic protocols."},{"line":3,"english":"Industry experience: She collaborated with a domestic manufacturer of advanced metering infrastructure systems (AMI) on a project for firmware delivery over PLC and wireless links in the distribution network during the period 2016–2018. In addition, she participated as a technical advisor in a project for upgrading a SCADA telemetry system for a water management company."},{"line":4,"english":"Notes: She is currently supervising four doctoral candidates and is actively seeking industrial partners for the application of the results of the SAFELINK project. She is interested exclusively in collaboration in the domain of industrial embedded systems security; she does not accept consulting outside this domain."}]}

{"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"TRANS-LPWAN is a cross-border project that develops a shared infrastructure for telemetry monitoring of the environment and industrial facilities in the border area of Serbia and Hungary. The main technical contribution of the team from the Faculty of Technical Sciences relates to the security layer: defining protocols for authenticated firmware delivery on devices deployed along the cross-border river banks of the Tisa, key management in an administratively heterogeneous environment with two different national network operators, and establishing a procedure for secure remote device upgrade without physical access. The project entails a pilot installation on 35 field nodes."}]}
